title: The Weakest Start That Survives the Dungeon
statement:
A dungeon is a grid of rooms. `dungeon[r][c]` is what happens when you **enter** the room: a **negative** number is damage (you lose that much health), a **positive** number is healing, `0` is nothing. You start in the **top-left** room and want to reach the **bottom-right** room, moving only **right** or **down**. The start room and the end room also count.

Your health must be **at least 1 after every room**. Return the **smallest starting health** with which you can reach the end by some path.

examples.explanation: Going right then down: -3, +5, -6 needs 5 at the start (5 - 3 = 2, 7, 1). Going down first needs 14.
Healing never lowers the minimum below 1: you only need 1.

hints.nudge: If you work from the start you do not know how much health you will need later. Work from the END instead: how much health do you need when you stand at the last room, just before entering it?
hints.pattern: Dynamic programming from the bottom-right corner back to the top-left: need[r][c] = the least health you must have when ENTERING room (r, c); it is max(1, min(need of the room to the right, need of the room below) - dungeon[r][c]).
hints.pseudocode:
need[last][last] = max(1, 1 - dungeon[last][last])
for r from the bottom up, for c from the right to the left: next = min(need[r + 1][c], need[r][c + 1]) (only the existing neighbours)
  need[r][c] = max(1, next - dungeon[r][c])
return need[0][0]
hints.walkthrough: A forward table 'best health so far' does not work: a path with a higher sum can be worse because it dips lower in the middle, and two partial paths cannot be compared by one number. Going backwards fixes this: define need[r][c] as the smallest health you must have when you ENTER room (r, c) so that you can finish. After the room you will have health h + dungeon[r][c], and that must be at least the smaller of the needs of the two rooms you can go to next. So h = (that smaller need) - dungeon[r][c], but you also need at least 1 to survive the room itself, so need[r][c] = max(1, next - dungeon[r][c]). The last room has no next room: it needs max(1, 1 - dungeon). Fill the table from the end to the start; the answer is need[0][0]. O(rows * columns).
